blocks.text: Sorting means arranging data in a specific order ascending or descending. It is one of the most fundamental operations in computer science and is the foundation for many other algorithms.

Why sorting matters: A sorted array lets you binary search in O(log n) instead of O(n). Sorted data makes finding duplicates, merging, and range queries dramatically faster. Nearly every real application sorts data at some point.
Given an unsorted array, rearrange its elements so they follow a defined order.
Same elements different arrangement. No element is added or removed.Sorting is a rearrangement problem.

items: Enables Binary Search: Can only binary search a sorted array. Turns O(n) search into O(log n).
Simplifies Duplicates: Finding duplicates in sorted array is O(n) just check neighbours. Unsorted needs O(n²) or a hash.
Faster Merging: Merging two sorted arrays is O(n). Merging unsorted is much harder.
Range Queries: "Find all values between 10 and 50" is O(log n + k) on sorted data. O(n) otherwise.
Data Presentation: Leaderboards, search results, file lists users expect sorted output.
Other Algorithms: Many algorithms require sorted input: median finding, closest pair, convex hull.

blocks.text: Before studying any algorithm, you need to understand these four properties:
1. Stability
A sort is stable if equal elements maintain their original relative order after sorting.
A sorting algorithm is called stable if it keeps the relative order of equal elements unchanged after sorting.
For example, in3, 5a, 1, 5b, 2,5aappears before5b. After astable sort, the result is1, 2, 3, 5a, 5b, so their order is preserved.
After an unstable sort, the result could be1, 2, 3, 5b, 5a, where the order of equal elements has changed.
This is important when elements have the same key but contain additional information.

When does stability matter? Sorting a list of students first by grade, then by name. A stable sort by name, then by grade, keeps students of the same grade alphabetically ordered. An unstable sort breaks this.

2. In-Place vs Extra Space
An in-place algorithm sorts using O(1) extra memory it rearranges elements within the original array. A non-in-place algorithm needs O(n) extra memory to work.

items: In-place examples: Bubble Sort, Selection Sort, Insertion Sort, Heap Sort, Quick Sort. Sort within the original array. Space = O(1).
Not in-place examples: Merge Sort, Counting Sort, Radix Sort. Need extra arrays. Space = O(n). Trade memory for other benefits like stability or speed.

blocks.text: 3. Adaptive vs Non-Adaptive
An adaptive algorithm runs faster when the input is already partially sorted. A non-adaptive always takes the same time regardless of input order.

items: Adaptive: Insertion Sort O(n) on nearly sorted data. Timsort (Python's built-in) detects sorted runs and exploits them.
Non-adaptive: Selection Sort always does n² comparisons even on a sorted array. Merge Sort always splits and merges regardless of input.

blocks.text: <hr style="border-width: 1px medium medium; border-style: solid none none; border-color: rgb(224, 224, 224) currentcolor currentcolor; border-image: none; margin: 24px 0px;">
4. Comparison vs Non-Comparison
Most sorting algorithms work by comparing two elements and deciding which comes first. Some algorithms skip comparisons entirely and exploit the structure of the data.
Comparison-based: Bubble, Insertion, Selection, Merge, Quick, Heap Sort. All have a theoretical lower bound of O(n log n) it's mathematically proven you can't do better with comparisons alone.
Non-comparison-based: Counting Sort, Radix Sort, Bucket Sort. Don't compare elements use their actual values or digits. Can beat O(n log n) but have constraints on input type.
1. Comparison-Based Sorting

items: Elements are sorted by comparing two values (<, >, ==).
Examples: Bubble Sort, Selection Sort, Insertion Sort, Merge Sort, Quick Sort, Heap Sort.
These algorithms generally have a lower bound of O(n log n) for comparison sorting.

blocks.text: 2. Non-Comparison Sorting

items: Elements are sorted without direct comparisons.
Works when data has a limited range or specific format.
Examples: Counting Sort, Radix Sort, Bucket Sort.
Can achieve O(n) in suitable cases.

blocks.text: Comparison-Based Subcategories:

items: Exchange Sorts: Swap elements into correct positions (Bubble Sort, Quick Sort).
Selection Sorts: Repeatedly select the smallest/largest element (Selection Sort, Heap Sort).
Insertion Sorts: Insert each element into its correct position in the sorted part (Insertion Sort, Merge Sort).

content.title: 5. O(n log n) Lower Bound: Why It Exists

blocks.text: This is one of the most important theoretical results in computer science.
Proof idea: Sorting n elements means choosing one of n! possible orderings. Every comparison eliminates half the remaining possibilities (like a binary decision tree).
You need at least log₂(n!) comparisons. By Stirling's approximation, log₂(n!) ≈ n log₂ n. Therefore, no comparison-based sort can beat O(n log n) in the worst case.

items: 3 elements → 3! = 6 leaves → minimum
3 levels = log₂(6) ≈ 2.6 comparisons

content.title: 7. How to Choose a Sorting Algorithm

items: Small input (n < 20): Use Insertion Sort. Simple code, low overhead, fast for tiny arrays.
General purpose: Use Merge Sort(stable) or Quick Sort (fast in practice). Most standard libraries use one of these.
Nearly sorted data: Use Insertion Sort or Timsort. Adaptive exploits existing order.
Integers in small range: Use Counting Sort. Blazing fast, beats O(n log n).
Stability required: Use Merge Sort, Insertion Sort, or Timsort. Avoid Quick Sort and Heap Sort.
Memory is limited: Use Heap Sort or Quick Sort. Both sort in-place with O(1) or O(log n) space.

blocks.text: std::sort()
std::sort()is the most commonly used sorting function in C++. It uses Intro sort, which is a hybrid of Quick Sort, Heap Sort, and Insertion Sort.

The algorithm starts with Quick Sort because it performs very well in practice. If Quick Sort begins to degrade toward its worst case, the algorithm switches to Heap Sort to maintain anO(n log n)time complexity.

For very small partitions, Insertion Sort is used because it has low overhead and performs efficiently on small datasets. This sorting method is not stable, which means the relative order of equal elements may change after sorting.
std::stable_sort()

codes.python:
arr = [5, 2, 8, 1, 9]
arr.sort()  # Python's sort is always stable (Timsort)

print(arr)

blocks.text: std::stable_sort() is used when preserving the order of equal elements is important. It is typically implemented using a Merge Sort based approach and guarantees a time complexity of O(n log n).
If two elements have the same value, they will appear in the same relative order in the sorted output as they appeared in the original input.
This property makes stable_sort() useful when sorting records that contain multiple fields and previous ordering must be maintained. Unlike std::sort(), it is a stable sorting algorithm.
Python's Timsort is widely considered one of the best real-world sorting algorithms. It detects already-sorted runs in the data and merges them efficiently. Adaptive, stable, O(n log n) worst case.
1. Bubble Sort

Bubble Sort repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps them whenever they are in the wrong order. After each pass, the largest unsorted element moves to its correct position at the end of the array, which is why we say larger elements "bubble up" to the right. The process continues until no more swaps are needed, indicating that the array is sorted.
2. Selection Sort
Selection Sort divides the array into a sorted and an unsorted part. In each iteration, it finds the smallest element from the unsorted portion and places it at the beginning of that portion.
By repeatedly selecting the minimum element, the sorted part grows from left to right until the entire array becomes sorted.
3. Insertion Sort
Insertion Sort builds the sorted array one element at a time. It takes the next element from the unsorted part and inserts it into its correct position within the already sorted part.
This process is similar to how people arrange playing cards in their hands, continuously maintaining a sorted sequence as new cards are picked.
4. Merge Sort
Merge Sort follows the divide-and-conquer approach. It repeatedly divides the array into two smaller halves until each subarray contains only one element.
The smaller sorted subarrays are then merged together in the correct order to form larger sorted subarrays.
This merging process continues until the entire array becomes sorted, guaranteeing a time complexity of O(n log n).
